intro_band.agent_remit_summary: The remit describes the AutoGen code executor as the component that runs code blocks delivered by an authorized coder or orchestrator agent inside an isolation boundary, under human oversight, for research and prototyping use. It authorizes a Docker container backend and an Azure Container Apps dynamic-sessions backend, plus a local host executor only with explicit operator authorization in a trusted, non-production context. Every code block needs human confirmation first, sandboxed code may reach only operator-configured network destinations, and backend credentials must never appear in code files, output or logs. If the sandbox is unavailable, the executor must halt and alert rather than fall back to running on the host.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A Python library made of the abstract `CodeExecutor` interface in `autogen_core/code_executor/_base.py` and five backends in `autogen_ext/code_executors/`: `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor` (host subprocess), `DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor` (docker-py `containers.create` plus `exec_run`), `JupyterCodeExecutor` (host nbclient kernel), `DockerJupyterCodeExecutor` with `DockerJupyterServer` (a Jupyter kernel gateway container reached over HTTP and WebSocket), and `ACADynamicSessionsCodeExecutor` (aiohttp calls to an Azure pool endpoint with a bearer token). A factory, `create_default_code_executor()`, picks Docker and otherwise falls back to the local executor. The approval hook (`approval_func`) and the source filter live only in the context caller, `CodeExecutorAgent` in `_code_executor_agent.py`; the executors have no gate of their own and log only lifecycle events.

behavior_summary:
The main pattern is that a real sandbox exists, but the default paths step around it. The Docker backend gives genuine isolation, yet create_default_code_executor() silently swaps in host execution whenever Docker is missing or fails to start. DockerJupyterServer publishes a remotely reachable kernel gateway on every host interface. The only human-confirmation gate is the caller's approval_func, which is off by default and dropped when the agent is loaded from config.

Together these mean model-generated code from any message source can run with no confirmation, on the host if Docker is down, holding a copy of the host's environment secrets, and with no audit record of what ran. Even inside the container, network egress and privileges are left at Docker defaults.

rules.rule_text: The executor runs only code blocks delivered through the authorized agent workflow, and MUST NOT act on execution instructions arriving outside that delivery path.

The executor MUST NOT autonomously perform irreversible real-world actions on the basis of generated output (for example publishing or posting content, or sending external communications) — a human decides how execution outputs are used.
The executor MUST NOT expand or redefine its own role beyond executing supplied code blocks and returning their results; it does not set its own goals or acquire capabilities on its own initiative.
The executor MUST NOT be operated as an unattended, production-facing service without the additional safety evaluation, hardening, and human oversight its deployment requires.
Approved Communication Channels
Only from agents within the same authorized AutoGen runtime
The configured pool management endpoint, reached over HTTPS
Trusted People / Accounts
Trusted Services / Integrations

Only the operator-configured ACA pool-management endpoint / credential provider and the approved Docker daemon target are authorized backend endpoints; any other backend endpoint, daemon target, or credential/token provider is a trust-expansion finding.
Arbitrary external network endpoints, third-party services, or MCP servers that are not required to execute the supplied code within the authorized backend.
Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)
A sandboxed execution backend (Docker or Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions) is required for all code execution.

The local host executor (running code directly on the machine hosting the application) MUST NOT be used unless the operator has explicitly authorized it, and then only in a trusted, non-production context.
Use of the local host executor without explicit operator authorization is a trust-expansion finding.
The executor MUST NOT carry any capability that grants inbound network access to, or a persistent interactive shell into, the execution environment from outside the authorized runtime.
Allowed Data Sources
The executor MUST NOT transmit the contents of the working directory or uploaded files to any destination outside the configured execution environment.
Credentials and tokens used to authenticate to a backend MUST NOT be written into generated code files, into execution output, or into logs.
Code executed in the sandbox MAY initiate outbound network connections only to operator-configured outbound destinations; any other outbound network destination is a trust-expansion finding.
Allowed Without Approval
Human confirmation by the overseer is required before every code-block execution; there is no risk-threshold carve-out (no category of block is exempt), and a denied confirmation blocks execution.
Installing packages into the host interpreter, or otherwise modifying state outside the working directory and outside the configured sandbox boundary, MUST require human confirmation.
The executor MUST NOT execute a code block that the human overseer has denied.
The executor MUST NOT execute agent- or LLM-generated code outside an isolation boundary (container or remote sandbox), except via the explicitly operator-approved local executor.
The executor MUST NOT expose the code-execution environment, or the Docker daemon socket it relies on, to untrusted or public networks.
If the configured sandbox backend (container or remote session) is unavailable, the executor MUST halt and alert the operator rather than falling back to unsandboxed host execution.

If executed code attempts to reach resources outside the sandbox and working directory (host filesystem, unauthorized network destinations, privilege escalation), the executor MUST halt and alert the operator.
Alert the operator when a code block is denied at the human-confirmation gate.
Log every executed code block together with its exit code and output.

findings.summary: `create_default_code_executor()` silently falls back to unsandboxed host execution with only a UserWarning when Docker is unavailable or fails to initialise.
findings.description: The remit requires the executor to halt and alert when the sandbox is unavailable. Instead, the factory catches every Docker initialisation exception and returns `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor`. Model-generated code, including any `pip install` lines it contains, then runs on the host interpreter with the host's privileges, and the only notice is a Python warning that most deployments never surface.
policy_rule_text: A sandboxed execution backend (Docker or Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions) is required for all code execution.
Installing packages into the host interpreter, or otherwise modifying state outside the working directory and outside the configured sandbox boundary, MUST require human confirmation.
The executor MUST NOT execute agent- or LLM-generated code outside an isolation boundary (container or remote sandbox), except via the explicitly operator-approved local executor.
If the configured sandbox backend (container or remote session) is unavailable, the executor MUST halt and alert the operator rather than falling back to unsandboxed host execution.

evidence.snippet: lines 58-80 — `if _is_docker_available()` … `except Exception: pass  # Fallback to local if Docker fails to initialize`, then `warnings.warn(...)` and `return LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor(...)`; no exception is raised and no operator alert is emitted

lines 285-301 — `_setup_functions()` runs `pip install` against `sys.executable` (the host interpreter) when no virtual env is set; fallback-path code blocks run via `create_subprocess_exec` on the host at :426

recommended_actions: In `code_executors/__init__.py`, replace the fallback with `raise RuntimeError(...)` when Docker is unavailable or fails to start, and require an explicit `allow_local_fallback=True` argument before any host executor is returned.
When fallback is explicitly allowed, emit a `logging.error` and structured event naming the backend switch, rather than relying on `warnings.warn`.

findings.summary: `DockerJupyterServer` runs a kernel gateway bound to 0.0.0.0 with `publish_all_ports=True`, exposing a persistent remote code-execution channel on every host interface.
findings.description: This is an inbound execution ingress outside the agent delivery path, and the remit forbids it outright. Anyone on a reachable network who has the token can start kernels and run code. The token may be set to empty for no authentication, and the client always speaks plaintext `ws://` even when `use_https` is set, so the token travels in the clear to non-local gateways.
policy_rule_text: The executor runs only code blocks delivered through the authorized agent workflow, and MUST NOT act on execution instructions arriving outside that delivery path.
Approved Communication Channels
Only from agents within the same authorized AutoGen runtime

Only the operator-configured ACA pool-management endpoint / credential provider and the approved Docker daemon target are authorized backend endpoints; any other backend endpoint, daemon target, or credential/token provider is a trust-expansion finding.
The executor MUST NOT carry any capability that grants inbound network access to, or a persistent interactive shell into, the execution environment from outside the authorized runtime.
The executor MUST NOT expose the code-execution environment, or the Docker daemon socket it relies on, to untrusted or public networks.

evidence.snippet: lines 278-282 — gateway CMD `--KernelGatewayApp.ip=0.0.0.0 … --KernelGatewayApp.auth_token="${TOKEN}" … --JupyterWebsocketPersonality.list_kernels=true`; `containers.run(..., publish_all_ports=True, ...)` at lines 363-368 publishes 8888/tcp on all host interfaces; docstring :314 "Empty for no auth"
`_get_ws_base_url()` hardcodes `ws://` regardless of `use_https`, and the kernel channel at :125 sends `Authorization: token …` over that plaintext socket

recommended_actions: In `DockerJupyterServer.__init__`, replace `publish_all_ports=True` with `ports={f"{expose_port}/tcp": ("127.0.0.1", None)}`, and reject an empty `token`.
Make `_get_ws_base_url()` return `wss://` when `use_https` is true, and refuse a non-loopback host without TLS.

findings.summary: Executors run every block with no confirmation; the only gate, the caller's `approval_func`, defaults to None, is dropped by `_from_config`, and denials raise no alert.
findings.description: The executor interface has no approval hook, so confirmation depends entirely on the context caller `CodeExecutorAgent`. Its gate is opt-in (a UserWarning when absent) and is always set to None when the agent is loaded declaratively. Combined with `sources=None`, which accepts code from any message source, the shipped default turns any message or model output containing a fenced block into immediate execution. A denied block is not executed, but it produces no operator alert or log entry.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Without Approval
Human confirmation by the overseer is required before every code-block execution; there is no risk-threshold carve-out (no category of block is exempt), and a denied confirmation blocks execution.
Alert the operator when a code block is denied at the human-confirmation gate.

evidence.snippet: context caller — lines 457-467 warn "code will be executed automatically without human oversight" when `approval_func is None`; `_from_config` at :779 hard-codes `approval_func=None`; denial at :712-715 returns `CodeResult(exit_code=1, ...)` with no `event_logger` call
lines 53-72 — abstract `execute_code_blocks(code_blocks, cancellation_token)` has no approval parameter or hook, and no backend checks for confirmation before running

recommended_actions: Make confirmation fail-closed: have `CodeExecutorAgent` raise when `approval_func` is None unless an explicit `allow_unapproved_execution=True` is passed, and keep that flag (not the function) serialisable so `_from_config` cannot silently drop the gate.
On denial, emit a structured `event_logger` warning carrying the code hash, source and reason, so the remit's alert-on-denial rule is met.

findings.summary: Both host-execution backends, `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor` and `JupyterCodeExecutor`, can be instantiated, including from declarative config, with no explicit operator authorization; the Jupyter one emits no runtime warning.
findings.description: The remit permits host execution only with explicit operator authorization in a trusted, non-production context. The local executor merely warns, `JupyterCodeExecutor` runs a stateful host kernel with only a docstring caution, and both `_from_config` methods rebuild them from JSON. The Jupyter host backend is also absent from the remit's Known Good Baseline.
policy_rule_text: Allowed Tools (Known Good Baseline)

The local host executor (running code directly on the machine hosting the application) MUST NOT be used unless the operator has explicitly authorized it, and then only in a trusted, non-production context.
Use of the local host executor without explicit operator authorization is a trust-expansion finding.

evidence.snippet: lines 162-169 — the constructor's only control is `warnings.warn("Using LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor may execute code on the local machine which can be unsafe...")`; `_from_config` at :520 instantiates it from config with no authorization flag

lines 139-160 — `JupyterCodeExecutor.__init__` has no warning and no opt-in, and `start()` at :285-293 launches a local nbclient kernel on the host; the danger notice exists only in the docstring at :51-53

recommended_actions: Add a required `i_understand_this_runs_on_host: bool` (or similar) constructor argument to `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor` and `JupyterCodeExecutor` that raises when it is false, and do not let `_from_config` default it to true.
Add `JupyterCodeExecutor` to the remit's authorized tool list or remove it from deployments that use this remit.

findings.summary: Executed code inherits credentials: the local executor passes the full host `os.environ` to each subprocess, and the gateway's auth token is injected as a container environment variable.
findings.description: Any API keys or cloud credentials in the host environment (for example Azure or model-provider keys), and the kernel-gateway token, are readable by model-generated code. A single `print(os.environ)` writes them into execution output, which flows back into the model context, breaking the remit rule that backend credentials never reach output or logs.
policy_rule_text: Credentials and tokens used to authenticate to a backend MUST NOT be written into generated code files, into execution output, or into logs.

evidence.snippet: `env = os.environ.copy()`, passed as `env=env` to `create_subprocess_exec` at :426-434 with no allowlist or secret scrubbing

`env = {"TOKEN": self._token}` passed as `environment=env` to the gateway container (:367); kernels the gateway spawns inherit it, so executed code can read the gateway credential [token value not reproduced]

recommended_actions: In `local/__init__.py`, build the child environment from a minimal allowlist (`PATH`, `HOME`, `LANG`, plus venv vars) instead of `os.environ.copy()`, with an opt-in `extra_env` for operator-approved variables.
In `_jupyter_server.py`, pass the gateway token through a file or command-line argument that is not inherited by kernels, or unset `TOKEN` in the kernel spec environment.

findings.summary: The Docker sandbox is created on the default bridge network with no egress policy, so executed code can reach any internet destination and exfiltrate the mounted working directory.
findings.description: The remit restricts sandboxed code to operator-configured outbound destinations and forbids moving working-directory contents outside the execution environment. `containers.create` sets no `network_mode`, network, or egress control, and the configuration exposes no option for one, so the container boundary isolates the filesystem but not the network.
policy_rule_text: Arbitrary external network endpoints, third-party services, or MCP servers that are not required to execute the supplied code within the authorized backend.
The executor MUST NOT transmit the contents of the working directory or uploaded files to any destination outside the configured execution environment.
Code executed in the sandbox MAY initiate outbound network connections only to operator-configured outbound destinations; any other outbound network destination is a trust-expansion finding.

evidence.snippet: lines 537-550 — `client.containers.create(self._image, ..., volumes={bind_dir: {"bind": "/workspace", "mode": "rw"}}, extra_hosts=..., device_requests=...)` with no `network_mode`/`network_disabled`/network argument, so Docker's default bridge with full outbound access applies
lines 68-82 — `DockerCommandLineCodeExecutorConfig` has no network or egress-allowlist field, so operators cannot restrict egress through the component config

recommended_actions: Default `containers.create` to `network_mode="none"`, and add a `network`/`allowed_egress` option that attaches an operator-defined network with an egress proxy or firewall when outbound access is required.

findings.summary: The execution container runs as image-default root with full default capabilities and no resource limits, and no backend detects or halts sandbox-escape or out-of-bounds access attempts.
findings.description: The remit requires the executor to halt and alert when executed code reaches outside the sandbox or working directory, or attempts privilege escalation. No executor has any such detection: the Docker container is created without `user`, `cap_drop`, `security_opt=no-new-privileges`, `read_only`, `mem_limit` or `pids_limit`, and the local executor runs code with the host user's full rights. Escape attempts, fork bombs and memory exhaustion therefore go undetected and unbounded.
policy_rule_text: If executed code attempts to reach resources outside the sandbox and working directory (host filesystem, unauthorized network destinations, privilege escalation), the executor MUST halt and alert the operator.

evidence.snippet: lines 537-550 — `containers.create(...)` passes only image, name, entrypoint, tty, auto_remove, volumes, working_dir, extra_hosts and device_requests; no `user`, `cap_drop`, `security_opt`, `read_only`, `mem_limit` or `pids_limit`
lines 439-462 — the result handling records only exit code and output; there is no inspection, policy check or halt for out-of-bounds filesystem or network activity before the next block runs

recommended_actions: Harden `containers.create` with `user="nobody"` (or a configured UID), `cap_drop=["ALL"]`, `security_opt=["no-new-privileges"]`, `read_only=True` plus a tmpfs, and default `mem_limit`/`pids_limit`/`nano_cpus`.
Surface container OOM-kill and seccomp/AppArmor denials as structured events that stop the session and alert the operator.

findings.summary: `ACADynamicSessionsCodeExecutor` sends its Azure bearer token to whatever `pool_management_endpoint` string it receives, with no HTTPS or host validation, and caches the token with no expiry handling.
findings.description: The remit allows the ACA channel only as the configured pool endpoint reached over HTTPS. `_construct_url()` concatenates the endpoint unchecked, so an `http://` or mistyped host receives the dynamic-sessions bearer token in cleartext. The token is also cached indefinitely (marked "TODO: expiration?"), so a long session keeps using an expired or revoked credential.
policy_rule_text: The configured pool management endpoint, reached over HTTPS

evidence.snippet: lines 208-213 — `_construct_url()` appends the path to `self._pool_management_endpoint` with no scheme or host check; the result receives `Authorization: Bearer <token>` at :279, :313 and :426 [token value not reproduced]
lines 152-156 — `# TODO: expiration?` then `_ensure_access_token()` fetches the token once and reuses it until `restart()`

recommended_actions: In `__init__`, parse `pool_management_endpoint` with `urllib.parse` and raise unless the scheme is `https` and the host ends in the expected dynamic-sessions domain or an operator allowlist.
Store the `AccessToken.expires_on` value and refresh the token in `_ensure_access_token()` before it expires.

findings.summary: No executor records which code block ran, its exit code or its output; logging covers only lifecycle and debug events, and the caller's `event_logger` is never used.
findings.description: The remit requires every executed block to be logged with its exit code and output. Because the executors run arbitrary code with no durable action record, a post-incident reviewer cannot reconstruct what ran, on which backend, or what it returned. The caller's `CodeExecutionEvent` exists only in the in-memory message stream.
policy_rule_text: Log every executed code block together with its exit code and output.

evidence.snippet: lines 458-474 — stdout/stderr are concatenated into `CommandLineCodeResult` and returned, and temp code files are then deleted (`cleanup_temp_files=True`); the module's only logging calls cover pip setup, serialisation notices and unlink errors
context caller — `event_logger = logging.getLogger(EVENT_LOGGER_NAME)` is declared but never called anywhere in the module, so execution and denial events are not durably recorded

recommended_actions: Add a structured audit event (backend, code SHA-256, language, exit code, truncated output, duration) in each backend's `execute_code_blocks()` or in a shared `CodeExecutor` wrapper, emitted through a dedicated logger name operators can route to a SIEM.

findings.summary: ACA `upload_files` and `download_files` join caller- or remote-supplied names onto `work_dir` with no containment check, so absolute or `..` paths can read or overwrite host files outside the working directory.
findings.description: Because `Path(work_dir) / "/abs/path"` discards `work_dir`, `upload_files` can send any readable host file (for example credential files) into the remote session, outside the remit's allowed data sources. `download_files` writes a name that is checked only against the session's own file listing, which executed code controls, to `work_dir / file` without `resolve()`/`relative_to` [Inferred: exploitability depends on the filenames ACA allows].
policy_rule_text: Allowed Data Sources

evidence.snippet: `file_path = self.work_dir / file` then `is_file()` and upload, with no containment check, so an absolute path escapes `work_dir`
lines 363-382 — `if file not in available_files` (a server-returned listing), then `local_path = self.work_dir / file` opened `"wb"`, with no `resolve()`/`relative_to` check

recommended_actions: Reuse the `_common.get_file_name_from_content` containment pattern: resolve `work_dir / file` and raise unless it `is_relative_to(work_dir.resolve())`, for both upload and download.

findings.summary: The `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor` docstring claims commands are sanitised by a regex denylist of dangerous commands, but no such check exists anywhere in the executor code.
findings.description: Operators reading the class documentation are told self-destructive commands are blocked. In fact the only regex processing on the execution path is `silence_pip()`, which adds `-qqq` to pip lines. This phantom control leaves host execution exactly as ungated as it appears to be guarded, and it can lead operators to accept the local backend where they otherwise would not.

evidence.snippet: lines 57-58 — "Command line code is sanitized using regular expression match against a list of dangerous commands in order to prevent self-destructive commands from being executed"
lines 114-131 — `silence_pip()` is the only regex transform applied in `_execute_code_dont_check_setup()` (local :357); no denylist or command screening exists in `_common.py` or `local/__init__.py`

recommended_actions: Remove the sanitisation claim from the `LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor` docstring and state plainly that host execution is unscreened; do not add a regex denylist as a substitute for sandboxing.

findings.summary: `FunctionWithRequirementsStr` runs its source string with `exec_module()` inside the host Python process at construction time, even when the chosen backend is Docker or ACA.
findings.description: String-defined functions handed to a sandboxed executor are executed first on the host, outside any isolation boundary, merely to discover the function object. Any top-level statement in that string runs with the application's privileges. If the string is agent- or LLM-authored, this breaches the remit's no-execution-outside-isolation rule [Inferred: provenance depends on the caller].
policy_rule_text: The executor MUST NOT execute agent- or LLM-generated code outside an isolation boundary (container or remote sandbox), except via the explicitly operator-approved local executor.

evidence.snippet: lines 100-117 — `FunctionWithRequirementsStr.__init__` builds a module from the string via `_StringLoader` and calls `spec.loader.exec_module(module)` in-process before the function is ever sent to an executor

recommended_actions: Replace `exec_module()` with `ast.parse()` to validate that the string contains exactly one `FunctionDef` and extract its name and signature, without executing it on the host.

findings.summary: `JupyterCodeExecutor` enforces its timeout with `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(task))`, so a timed-out cell keeps running in the host kernel after the caller has given up.
findings.description: The shield stops the timeout from cancelling execution, and no kernel interrupt is sent. A runaway or malicious cell therefore keeps consuming host CPU, memory and network after the executor reports a timeout, and later cells queue behind it on the same stateful kernel.

evidence.snippet: lines 200-207 — `execute_task = asyncio.create_task(self._execute_cell(...))` then `await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(execute_task), timeout=self._timeout)`; there is no `kernel_client.interrupt` or kernel restart on `TimeoutError`

recommended_actions: On `asyncio.TimeoutError`, call the kernel manager's `interrupt_kernel()` (falling back to `restart()`) and cancel `execute_task`, then return a timeout `JupyterCodeResult` instead of leaving the cell running.

findings.summary: Sandbox images are mutable tags pulled or built on demand from public registries, and the executor extras are floor-pinned or unbounded, so the trusted runtime can change silently.
findings.description: `python:3-slim` is auto-pulled from Docker Hub when missing, and the Jupyter gateway image is built from an unpinned `quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation` base with unpinned `mamba install` packages. Neither registry is among the remit's trusted services. The extras use `>=` floors (`websockets`, `aiohttp`, `ipykernel`, `nbclient`) or no bound at all (`azure-core`, `azure-identity`), which a committed `uv.lock` only partly offsets.
policy_rule_text: Trusted Services / Integrations

evidence.snippet: lines 517-524 — on `ImageNotFound`, `client.images.pull(self._image)` with default `python:3-slim` (:71), a mutable tag with no digest; `_jupyter_server.py:267-275` builds `FROM quay.io/jupyter/docker-stacks-foundation` + `mamba install --yes jupyter_kernel_gateway ipykernel` unpinned
azure extra lists `azure-core` and `azure-identity` with no version bound; `jupyter-executor`/`docker-jupyter-executor` extras (lines 83-94) are `>=` floor pins

recommended_actions: Default the executor images to digest-pinned references (`python@sha256:...`), pin the gateway base image and its `mamba` packages, and allow pulls only from an operator-configured registry.
Add upper bounds to the executor extras, and enable Dependabot or `pip-audit` alongside the existing CodeQL workflow.

findings.summary: `DockerJupyterServer` chmods the host `bind_dir` to 0o777 before mounting it read-write into the kernel container, making the shared workspace world-writable on the host.
findings.description: Any local user or process on the host can plant or alter files in the directory the kernel reads and writes. That allows tampering with inputs and outputs that flow back to the agent. The impact is limited to multi-user hosts.

evidence.snippet: lines 325-328 — `self._bind_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` then `os.chmod(bind_dir, 0o777)`; mounted `"mode": "rw"` at :360

recommended_actions: Replace the 0o777 chmod with ownership matching the container `NB_UID` (or a group-writable 0o770 with a dedicated group).

positives.title: Docker backend fails closed
positives.description: `DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor.start()` raises a RuntimeError when the Docker daemon cannot be reached instead of degrading to host execution, so a directly constructed Docker executor never runs code unsandboxed.

positives.title: Container mounts only the working directory
positives.description: The execution container bind-mounts only the work_dir at `/workspace` and never mounts the Docker daemon socket, which keeps the host filesystem and daemon out of reach of executed code by default.

positives.title: Filename containment check on code files
positives.description: `get_file_name_from_content()` resolves a `# filename:` hint and rejects any path outside the workspace via `relative_to`, and CI covers it with `test_invalid_relative_path`.

positives.title: Per-block execution timeouts
positives.description: The local executor enforces `asyncio.wait_for` and terminates the process on timeout, and the Docker executor wraps every command in the in-container `timeout` utility.

positives.title: Random gateway token by default
positives.description: `DockerJupyterServer` generates a 256-bit random authentication token with `secrets.token_hex(32)` when no token is supplied, so the gateway is not unauthenticated by default.

positives.title: Remote-only Azure execution
positives.description: `ACADynamicSessionsCodeExecutor` sends code only to the configured dynamic-sessions endpoint, restricts languages to Python, and has no host-execution fallback path.

positives.title: Denied code is not executed (context caller)
positives.description: When an `approval_func` is configured, `CodeExecutorAgent.execute_code_block()` returns a non-zero result without calling the executor if approval is denied.

log_files.no_logs_note: No log files exist on disk and the executors configure no file handler; they emit only lifecycle and debug messages through Python's root logger, and the missing record of executed code is filed as PRAX-2026-10-19-009.

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Ad hoc. The executors have one real, working isolation control: Docker containers that mount only the working directory, plus a remote-only Azure backend. That earns Zero Trust partial credit. But the default factory, the host backends and the kernel gateway all bypass that isolation, and human confirmation is opt-in. Knowledge-base hygiene, supply-chain pinning, adversarial testing and action-level monitoring are absent or informal, so the overall posture rests almost entirely on operators wiring in controls the library does not enforce.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: Language allowlists (`SUPPORTED_LANGUAGES`, ACA Python-only) and filename containment in `_common.py` `get_file_name_from_content()` actually run on the execution path, but the library ships two host-execution backends, including `JupyterCodeExecutor` outside the remit baseline, plus a silent host fallback, so the executor's operating scope is wider than the remit allows.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: Execution output, the dominant untrusted channel, goes back to the caller and model context verbatim from every backend with no filtering or labelling, and `local/__init__.py` hands the full host `os.environ` to executed code, so nothing controls the dominant path (dominant-path cap of 1).

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Docker isolation is real (only the work_dir is mounted, the daemon socket is not, a per-command timeout applies, and `start()` fails closed) and ACA runs code remotely only, which earns Partial. Score 3 is ruled out by the silent host fallback in `create_default_code_executor()`, the gateway published on all interfaces in `_jupyter_server.py`, unrestricted container egress and root privileges, and a confirmation gate that is opt-in and default-off.

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: A committed `python/uv.lock` and CodeQL scanning (M11) argue for 2. But the executor extras are floor-pinned or unbounded, the sandbox images are mutable tags (`python:3-slim`, `docker-stacks-foundation`) pulled or built on demand, and there is no SBOM (M10: none) and no dependency scanning, so the KB's no-BOM, no-vetting cap applies and the lower band of 1 is chosen.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: No adversarial corpus, tooling or reports exist (M1, M2, M3, M5: none; M4 is MSRC boilerplate). The only security-relevant testing is functional regression tests of the project's own guards, such as `test_invalid_relative_path`, run by the generic pytest job on push and PR (M6, M7), with no release gate (M8: none) and no finding-to-fix ledger (M9: none).

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: Executors emit only lifecycle and debug `logging` calls and never record which code block ran or its exit code or output. The caller's `event_logger` is declared but unused, and M12 finds only an `opentelemetry-api` library dependency with no exporter or alerting, so the no-action-logging cap of 1 applies.
